chronology: [Recap] Steelhead defeats Aghnar across dimensions, mutilates Honorata, drives Aghnar and Oda to suicide with internal mini-bombs, defeats dimensional vampires that breached reality through the battle-rift, and assassinates Don Nicanor Rosamel de Rokha on Philodendra to remove the only blocking vote.

[p01-p04] Investiture ceremony for the Medallion of High Nobility is interrupted by Dona Vicenta Gabriela de Rokha, who presents her father's remains as evidence of murder and casts a dissenting vote. Steelhead physically overpowers her, orders her safely returned to Philodendra, and vows to destroy the Golden Planet after he learns what love is.

[p05] Steelhead searches more than 3,500 planets and satellites for written knowledge of love; the Central Brain sends him to Terra Prima's omni-library. Ancient paper crumbles at his metal touch and he destroys the library in frustration.

[p06-p07] An accidental collision at the Metabunker activates a signal-detection machine that projects a man reciting love poetry. Tonto traces the signal to a tiny planet at the galaxy's edge identified as the home of Zaran Krleza, the last poet believed dead for 5,000 years. The ship sets course.

[p08-p09] Steelhead survives acid storms and pachydermic jellyfish to reach Zaran Krleza's fortress. A voice inside greets him as a long-awaited culmination and refuses forced entry; it demands a soul trial instead.

[p10-p12] The trial assigns Steelhead an ancient bow without arrows and forbids killing the octo-tiger opponent. Brute force fails. He produces a musical note with the bow, soothes the creature to sleep, and passes by imagination rather than violence.

[p13] Inside the fortress Steelhead finds a surviving poet-head, the last remnant of Zaran Krleza, suspended in machinery. An ancient cable-bound being says it has waited five thousand years and that emotions cannot be taught directly.
[p14] Steelhead and Zaran Krleza's head agree to merge. Endo-robots perform a full nerve, vein, and artery surgical fusion without anesthetic, erasing both prior egos and producing a new being.

[p15] The new being names himself Melmoth, declares love for Dona Vicenta Gabriela de Rokha, and states his intent to father an heir. Tonto warns that his past violence against her family makes the plan impossible.

[p16-p19] Melmoth travels to Gzayn in the Dark Galaxy, fights through its macromite temple, kills all 72,000 defenders, triggers the buried self-destruct switch, and extracts the Halerce tree and its Djy-ouk birds in a containment cylinder before the planet's end.

[p20-p21] On Philodendra at dawn, Dona Vicenta wakes to impossible Djy-ouk birdsong, finds her Imperial Endoguards unconscious, and sees the Halerce tree standing where a scorched hole stood the day before. Tonto identifies Melmoth as responsible and describes the gift as an act of love.

[p22-p24] Dona Vicenta meets Melmoth in a radiant golden environment and is moved by him before learning he murdered her father. She declares she loves and hates him simultaneously. Melmoth offers her the Castaka paleo-revolver and urges her to take revenge. The volume closes before she fires; the next episode is announced as Melmoth's Plight.

[p26-p30, supplemental] Young visor-wearing conspirators stage a coup aboard a ship, confront an elderly white-robed figure who disperses rather than dying, are captured by a giant serpent, and are condemned by a tribunal ordering memory extraction. A supreme techno-priest oversees rehabilitation of the three captives. Narrative connection to the main Metabarons story is not established in this volume.
locations: Imperial Palace (prior arc; site of dimensional vampire invasion)
Philodendra — Troglosocialik capital; home of Dona Vicenta Gabriela de Rokha; delivery site for the Halerce tree gift
The Golden Planet — imperial seat with nobles and an empress; Steelhead's stated future target
Terra Prima — humanity's cradle; location of the omni-library with disintegrating ancient paper
The Metabunker — Steelhead/Melmoth's base; houses Tonto, ant-robots, and the signal-detection machine
Galaxy's edge planet — site of acid storms, pachydermic jellyfish, and Zaran Krleza's fortress
Zaran Krleza's fortress — sealed structure requiring a soul trial for entry; interior chamber holds the poet's suspended head amid mechanical remains
Gzayn — central planet of the Dark Galaxy; location of the Halerce tree, macromite temple, and buried self-destruct switch
lore_laws: The Medallion of High Nobility requires a unanimous ambassadorial vote; one dissent blocks the award.
Cross-dimensional combat can tear open breaches admitting hostile entities into the universe.
Mini-bombs implanted in bodies can be detonated for suicide.
The Pthagureans are capable of collective suicide and can decree or halt it.
Terra Prima is humanity's cradle; its omni-library exists but ancient paper there disintegrates on contact.
Zaran Krleza is the last known poet; poetry is considered galaxy-wide extinct; he had been missing approximately 5,000 years.
The galaxy's edge planet has acid winds, crushing atmospheric pressure requiring multi-ton exoskeletons, and is compared to mythological hell.
Forcing entry into Zaran Krleza's fortress would destroy the entire planet.
The fortress soul trial requires defeating the octo-tiger without killing it; breaking the rules risks planetary destruction.
Endo-robots can surgically fuse a separate head and body by splicing nerves, veins, and arteries; the procedure erases both prior egos.

Gzayn, the central planet of the Dark Galaxy, hosts macromites that devour human flesh; its Halerce tree is approximately 370,000 years old and shelters 9 million Djy-ouk birds behind an indestructible astro-fiber barrier with a buried self-destruct mechanism.
The Castakas possess a traditional ceremonial firearm called a paleo-revolver.
Memory-extraction technology exists and can erase identity through imposed virtual memories, used here as both punishment and rehabilitation.
major_events: Dona Vicenta Gabriela de Rokha interrupts Steelhead's investiture, presents her father's remains, and casts the vote that blocks the Medallion of High Nobility.
Steelhead's search across more than 3,500 worlds fails; he destroys Terra Prima's omni-library in rage.
Tonto traces an accidental signal to Zaran Krleza, the last poet, alive at the galaxy's edge after 5,000 years.
Steelhead passes the soul trial at Zaran Krleza's fortress by using music to pacify the octo-tiger without killing it.
Steelhead and Zaran Krleza's surviving head are surgically fused by endo-robots, erasing both prior egos and producing the new being Melmoth.
Melmoth massacres 72,000 macromites on Gzayn, triggers the temple self-destruct, and recovers the Halerce tree and its Djy-ouk birds.
Melmoth delivers the Halerce tree to Philodendra, neutralizes the Imperial Endoguards, and forces a confrontation with Dona Vicenta.
Dona Vicenta learns Melmoth killed her father; he gives her a Castaka paleo-revolver for vengeance; outcome deferred to Melmoth's Plight.
open_uncertainties: Whether Dona Vicenta will use the Castaka paleo-revolver on Melmoth or grant forgiveness — deferred to Melmoth's Plight.
The degree to which Steelhead's memories and ruthlessness survive within Melmoth versus being erased by the ego-dissolution surgery.
Whether Melmoth's claimed capacity for love is genuine or an artifact of the poet-head's influence inside the merged being.
The supplemental ship-coup narrative (p26-p30) has no established connection to the main Metabarons story within this volume; it may be an in-issue preview for The Technopriests.

Spelling and exact forms of recurring proper nouns remain uncertain across multiple pages: Pthagureans, Troglosocialik, Halerce/Hallerce/Halecre, Dyukka/Djy-ouk birds, macromites, Zaran Krleza/Kleza/Kreza.
Steelhead's public vow to destroy the Golden Planet and its empress is not acted upon within this volume.
recurring_motifs: Love as a capacity the mechanical warrior must earn through ordeal rather than possess by nature
Violent means used in pursuit of tender ends — Steelhead's path to love runs through killing and destruction at every stage
Transformation and rebirth through ego-dissolving surgery or bodily sacrifice
Ancient and supposedly extinct things — poets, birds, trees — surviving hidden in diminished forms
Soul trial versus strength trial as competing criteria for worthiness
The Metabaron lineage as a dynastic imperative that overrides personal feeling
Public ceremony corrupted or disrupted by private grievance
Youth against age as a site of power struggle, echoed in both the main story and the supplemental ship-coup narrative
title: Steelhead's Quest
